11556-facing-the-flag:
Jules Verne's Facing the Flag, in an anonymous American translation first published in 1897, opens at Healthful House, where Count d'Artigas appears and a kidnapping follows. The schooner Ebba carries the captives to sea, and Simon Hart, the engineer, keeps notes on where he is.

Back Cup, a hidden grotto, holds the secret at the heart of the tale, with Ker Karraje and Engineer Serko among its people. Verne compares the grotto with caves in Kentucky, Belgium, and elsewhere, counting domes, rivers, and cataracts. The novel is a scientific romance of invention, capture, and escape.
12449-a-reputed-changeling-or-three-seve:
Charlotte M. Yonge's tale, A Reputed Changeling, opens at Winchester. Two little girls walk home from a school kept by Frenchwomen, refugees before the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes. Talk of fairies, Gay's verses and Mother Goose tales frame a boy called ugly and ill-favoured, like Riquet with the tuft.

Is he a changeling, left by fairies in place of a stolen child, the girls ask. The novel follows three periods of seven years, testing that fancy against family life, faith and character. Yonge writes a historical tale for young readers, gentle in tone and fond of old Winchester. The changeling idea becomes a way to ask what makes a child truly one's own.
16407-under-the-dragon-flag:
James Allan, a Lancashire man who came into a large fortune young, tells what he saw and did in the war between China and Japan. He writes plainly, with no claim to fine style, and sets down scenes he took part in rather than a full history of the war. The book opens with his own back story, then moves to the fighting.

Readers get a first-hand view of a war that few English writers covered from the ground. Allan notes the odd chances that put him there, the sights of camp and battle, and the strain of life far from home. The result is a frank memoir of one man's war, told in his own unadorned voice.
19899-the-honour-of-the-flag:
W. W. Jacobs wrote The Honour of the Flag, a tale of the London river. Its man of business flourished for years in the East End. Having saved enough for his daily needs, he retired. He built a villa near the pleasant little town of Erith. The house overlooked the water. A considerable garden sloped down in front of it. Jacobs sets Thames-side comfort before his comedy starts.

Jacobs is best known for The Monkey's Paw and his night-watchman tales. His humor runs on sailors, skippers, and sly reversals. A flag's honour gives him patriotic cloth to cut comically. Erith and the river were his home waters. The tale shows his easy, exact storytelling. Few English humorists place a scene better.
23447-uncle-sam-s-boys-in-the-philippine:
H. Irving Hancock wrote this nineteen twelve boys' adventure of Uncle Sam's boys in the Philippines, following the flag against the Moros. The lads serve in the ranks, meet a Filipino dandy, gather at nipa barracks, and find plotters travelling with the flag.

Cervera's innocent shop, raids, and jungle fighting fill the chapters, with a frontispiece scene where an officer waves off a corporal's aid. Hancock writes for boys who love drill, duty, and daring, with clear talk of army life and island service. Readers should note the period view of empire and its foes, plain in the text, while enjoying the pace, the comradeship, and the young soldiers' grit under fire.
23476-churchwardens-manual-their-duties-:
George Henry, bishop of Guildford and archdeacon of Winchester, wrote this churchwardens' manual on their duties, powers, rights, and privileges, in a third edition from Simpkin and Company. A second edition had been called for within months of the first, a sign it met a want felt by clergy and wardens alike.

The manual was revised with new matter on burial laws, district churches and their mother church, and the transfer of land or buildings to trustees for mission work. Plain, orderly chapters tell wardens what they may do, must do, and must not do, from fabric and funds to burials and trusts. Church officers and historians will find a clear guide to a small but vital office in English parish life.
23485-the-old-man-s-bag:
T. W. H. Crosland and J. R. Monsell made this Dumpy Book for Children, number twenty two in the series, about an old man who lived in a wood with his wife and a quite large bag. One day he takes the bag on a walk, sees a hen in a field, and calls chuck, chuck.

The hen comes, and he pops her into the bag despite her great to do. More creatures and scrapes follow. A red policeman gives pursuit, a wife takes the bag down, and there is talk of cheap butter, apples knocked off a tree, and a suit measured for a soldier. The tale stays brisk and comic, with pictures for each turn. Small children will laugh at the bag that keeps filling and at the old man's cheerful cheek.
25188-the-flag:
Homer Greene's Flag, published in Philadelphia in 1917, is a patriotic novel that opens in a snow-covered village at a house called Bannerhall. A boy named Pen runs down the porch steps while his Aunt Millicent calls him back with news of his grandfather's train.

Family pride, a disputed tree, and a colonel's honor drive the home chapters, while later illustrations point to war service in France. Greene ties the flag to duty, sacrifice, and the older generation's example. The book speaks to American readers in the year the nation entered the First World War.
27745-the-true-story-of-the-american-fla:
John H. Fow published this 1908 study in Philadelphia with William J. Campbell, arguing that the true story of the American flag is more modest than popular legend. He opens with Rear-Admiral Preble's admission that Congress's records are silent on who designed the union of stars.

Fow traces colored stripes used for a common purpose nearly two hundred years before independence, and stars on a Massachusetts privateer's flag in November 1775. He holds that thirteen stripes were sentiment, not symbolism, and that stripe colors carry no fixed meaning beyond what imagination supplies.
2883-the-gold-bag:
Carolyn Wells wrote The Gold Bag as a detective novel narrated by a young but fairly experienced investigator. The crime at West Sedgwick opens the case, and chapters follow the Crawford house, the coroner's jury, the inquest, Florence Lloyd, and a gold bag found with yellow roses. A will, a midnight train, and the detective Fleming Stone all figure before the disclosure.

Suspicion falls on a beautiful girl whose fortune and lover seem to arrive with the crime itself, yet Philip Crawford insists she is neither principal nor accessory. A gold purse and two petals of a yellow rose mislead the jury. The novel pleases readers who enjoy a classic puzzle with romance, wills, and a careful untying of clues.
30288-sight-gag:
Larry M. Harris tells Sight Gag in Analog, May 1962, with pictures by Schoenherr. The tagline warns that brains help survival greatly, yet brains without muscle serve even worse than muscle without brains, and plain force is easily forgotten. Downstairs, the hotel register tells Fredericks that Mr. John P. Jones occupies Room 1014, but Fredericks does not believe the register and knows better.

Wherever his man is, he is not in Room 1014, and his real name is certainly not John P. Jones. Fredericks first met him under the name William K. Brady, as FBI Operative 71-054P, and wonders whether the K stands for killer. Operatives like Jones-Brady-X have as many names as jobs, and special talents, psi powers, make Fredericks mutter superman as a curse. Upstairs, in Room 1212, the superman sits and tries to relax.
30829-our-young-folks-vol-i-no-ii-februa:
Ticknor and Fields of Boston issued this February 1865 number, volume one, number two, of Our Young Folks, an illustrated magazine for boys and girls. The issue opens with David Matson, a New England tale told in prose, which its narrator links to Tennyson's Enoch Arden. In that poem a sailor returns from a desert island to find his wife wed to another man, and he keeps silent rather than cause her pain.

The magazine's own tale, the narrator says, is a similar story from his own neighborhood, about a man who left a young wife and little daughter for the sea. Young readers in 1865 would have found adventure, moral feeling, and pictures in one monthly parcel. Today the issue offers a clear view of Civil War era children's reading, in the plain, earnest style of its day.
30893-the-little-book-of-the-flag:
Eva March Tappan wrote this 1917 history of the American flag, published by Houghton Mifflin in Boston, New York, Chicago, Dallas, and San Francisco, and printed at the Riverside Press in Cambridge. Its chapters trace the flags that brought the colonists, the pine-tree flag and others, liberty and liberty poles, the land of many flags, Washington at Cambridge, and the Grand Union Flag.

Early chapters cover the English ancient flag, the meteor flag or Union Jack, Endicott cutting the cross from the flag, a flagless fort, and Dr. Cotton's decision on the cross. Later ones treat the Bedford flag, Sergeant Jasper saving the flag, the rattlesnake design, and the Philadelphia Light Horse Troop. It is a clear, patriotic history for young readers, told flag by flag.
32319-the-trail-of-the-sandhill-stag:
Ernest Thompson Seton's The Trail of the Sandhill Stag, with sixty drawings, was published in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons. Its copyright dates from 1899, with impressions running to December 1913. Seton, naturalist to the government of Manitoba and author of Wild Animals I Have Known, dedicates the book to the old-timers of Manitoba. Mrs. Grace Gallatin Thompson Seton did its designs for title-page, cover, and general make-up, and its literary revision.

To the reader, Seton writes simply: these are the best days of my life, these are my golden days. Its full-page drawings include The Track of a Mother Blacktail suddenly joined by two little ones' tracks, and The Trail in Spring. They continue with Wingless Birds, Sat Down in the Moonlit Snow, Seven Deer with their leader a wonderful buck, and The Doe Walking Slowly. Readers get a stag-tracking story from the Manitoba plain.
33154-the-telephone-an-account-of-the-ph:
Professor A. E. Dolbear of Tufts College wrote The Telephone in 1877. It is an account of electricity, magnetism, and sound as involved in the telephone's action, with directions for making a speaking telephone. Dolbear, author of The Art of Projecting, notes in his preface that popular exhibitions of the speaking telephone during the past six months, with newspaper articles, had created widespread interest. The interest was in the instrument. His book answers that interest with science a reader could test.

The volume explains the phenomena behind the telephone in plain terms, then tells how to build one. A student or amateur could hear the new wonder work in his own hands. As a record of the telephone's first year, it captures a moment when a marvel became a machine, and when readers wanted to understand it, not merely admire it.
35450-our-cats-and-all-about-them-their-:
Our Cats and All About Them is a book on the house cat by Harrison Weir. A new form of it was put out at London in eighteen ninety two. Its bill tells its whole aim in a line. Kinds, ways, and care of the cat are its theme. For the show bench it gives the mark of the best form and grace.

The book is sworn to the dear wife of the hand. It owns her soft, kind care for all beast life. The cat stands first in that care. The first words of the book tell its root. Notes and plates of the cat are the fruit of past fifty years of keen watch. From a small child to this day, the love of the wild world has been the chief joy of the hand.
36035-st-nicholas-vol-xiii-september-188:
Saint Nicholas was an illustrated magazine for young people, published by the Century Company of New York. This copy is volume 13, number 11, dated September 1886. An engraving after Landseer's painting The Connoisseurs stands at the front, with the painter's dogs at their study.

The lead article is Stories of Art and Artists, by Clara Erskine Clement, and this part treats the English painters. It opens with Henry the Eighth, a prince who loved pomp and called foreign artists to his court. Queen Elizabeth's long reign gave painters work but kept most of them foreign. King Charles the First loved art truly, with Rubens and Vandyck at his court and Inigo Jones as his architect. Clement argues that before Hogarth, portrait work was near the whole of English painting. Young readers got art history told as story.
39454-ahead-of-the-show-or-the-adventure:
Fred Thorpe wrote Ahead of the Show, or The Adventures of Al Allston, Advance Agent. The tale is Number Seventy Seven in the Bound to Win Library. Street and Smith held it at New York in 1897. Thorpe had writ Blind Luck and Chris, the Comedian. Thirty chapters carry the tale, most named for Al and his acts.

Al seeks a post, talks business, and forms a scheme in the first chapters. A rescue, a reward, and a rock ahead follow in swift turns. A mayor, peril, and a press talk fill the middle. An ad, a shadow rescue, and a lesson in journalism build the pace. A locket, a brother and sister, and a catastrophe mark the late plot. The book is a brisk dime novel of show life on the road.
39665-a-history-of-the-gipsies-with-spec:
A History of the Gipsies, with specimens of the Gipsy language, is a work of history and philology on the Romani people. The transcriber's notes to this copy explain its conventions: italics and small capitals as printed, breves and macrons shown by signs, and the oe-ligature written out. Tables were split or rearranged to fit the width of the page. Footnotes stand beneath the paragraphs they belong to.

A verse quoted in a passage preserved in the copy pictures its subjects. Hast thou not noted on the bye wayside, where aged willows lean over the lazy tide, a vagrant crew straggled through the glade? Their children loll round them on the grass, or pester the patient ass with their sports. The history traces the Gipsies' wanderings into Europe and their life in Britain.
40451-under-one-flag:
Under One Flag is a book of short stories by Richard Marsh, the author of The Beetle. John Long published it in London, where it first appeared in 1906. The collection holds fourteen tales, by turns comic, sentimental and strange.

The titles sketch the range: A Pet of the Ballet, A Christmas Miracle, Our Musical Comedy, My Wedding Day, and Two of a Trade. Then come Rewarded, On the River, A Member of the Anti-Tobacco League, An Episcopal Scandal, For Debt, and The Thirteen Club. The first story opens on a ballet girl ruefully studying her white satin shoes. Ballet ladies had to provide their own shoes, and she has twice sewn on fresh uppers. Now uppers and soles are both gone, money is shorter than ever, and she wonders whether clever patching will make them last till payday.
54891-historical-record-of-the-first-or-:
The Historical Record of the First, or Royal Regiment of Dragoons stands in the official British Army regimental history series. William Clowes and Sons printed it at London. Like its fellows, the volume opens with the general order issued at Horse Guards on January 1, 1836. In that order the king directed that an account of the services of every regiment be published. The Adjutant-General was to direct the whole.

The order fixed each record's contents. First came the regiment's formation and the circumstances of it. Then its stations, battles, sieges, and operations. Achievements were to be specified, with trophies captured from the enemy. Killed and wounded were to be listed, with place and date. Gallant officers and men were to be named, with their titles and medals. The badges and devices it bears close the account.
57047-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-2-no:
Captain Billy's Whiz Bang for May 1921 is one monthly number of an American joke magazine, volume two, number twenty. A sworn statement of ownership at the front gives its legal facts. The magazine was published monthly at Robbinsdale, Minnesota, the statement says. Harvey Fawcett swore to the form as its business manager, before a notary of his county.

Such statements were required by an act of congress of 1912 for all matter sent by mail. Behind that dry front stood one of the best loved humor magazines of its age. Whiz Bang mixed jokes, verse, and small town wit in a pocket sized monthly. Its success in these years founded the Fawcett publishing house, which grew from this Minnesota joke book into a giant of American magazines.
58229-humanity-to-honey-bees-or-practica:
Humanity to Honey Bees, by Thomas Nutt, is a guide to the care of bees on a kind, safe plan, in a second edition printed at Wisbech in 1834. Nutt promises that bee lives can be spared while honey of the best quality is gained in plenty. The book cost ten shillings.

Nutt gives the book, by leave, to Queen Adelaide. A Latin line from Virgil heads the title, on a seat and station to be sought for bees. He also sold honey made on his plan, plus hives stocked or unstocked, through an agent in High Holborn, London. His system used boxes and cottage hives under what he calls an admirable government in each colony. Bee keepers get an early humane method, set out step by step.
5869-michael-s-crag:
Michael's Crag opens with a Cornish landlord and a question about a bleak place. Eustace Le Neve asks Tyrrel, musingly, whether he cares for the place himself, while gazing across a long gray moor and a wide expanse of black and stormy water. The upland plateau about the Lizard promontory seems bleak and cold, Le Neve grants, yet the question hints at attachment beneath the bleakness.

Readers enter a Cornish romance of moors, sea, and property, where landscape shapes character and choice. The novel favors atmosphere and dialogue, letting a single exchange open questions of home, duty, and love. It suits readers who enjoy regional fiction, Cornish settings, and stories where a crag and a coast become characters in their own right.
59390-the-life-of-sir-rowland-hill-and-t:
The Life of Sir Rowland Hill, volume one, is the postal reformer's biography by himself and his nephew, published in 1880. Rowland Hill had begun the work after his retirement, writing the history of his great reform and a memoir of his early life. His nephew completed and edited the book after his death.

The dedication to Gladstone quotes the private journal: Hill recording, with emotion he could hardly suppress, his gratitude for Gladstone's uniform kindness and support in a time of great trouble. The preface tells how the worn-out reformer took up the history as the happiness of hard work, hoping to bring it out himself. The volume is both autobiography and archive: the story of the penny post told by the man who invented it, from inside his own papers.
59823-the-white-flag:
The White Flag is a tale by Gene Stratton-Porter. It was put out in nineteen twenty three at New York and at a town of the north land. A front plate by a named hand stands in the book. The book is sworn to the boys and girls grown tall of its day. With them, in child days, the hand says, she past past the white flag. Her past books are list at the front in three heaps.

The first heap is her books of the wild world. The song of a red bird, home with the birds, and birds of the great book stand in it. The song of the wild, friends in plumes, and the moths of a famed swamp fill that heap.
60604-under-honour-s-flag:
Eric Lisle, a clergyman, wrote this boys' school story, Under Honour's Flag, with pictures by G H Evison. The hero is Ralph, whose first day at school comes early in the contents. A true friend, Mr St Clive, proves himself in the third chapter. Horace Elgert, who strikes a savage blow in the front picture, causes much of the strife.

Chapter heads trace a plot of blame and honour at school. A strange affair leads to a cruel charge against Ralph, and things look black for him. A stolen banknote, a lost pocket-book, and a midnight visitor deepen the puzzle. Later heads promise the plot's failure and the truth about where the banknote went.
60787-old-shag:
Old Shag is a short tale of rail life by Bob Farnham. It first ran in a science fiction magazine in March of nineteen sixty. A tag line hints that a shaggy helper turns a hard spot for the hero. The tale is told as a yarn spun over a beer in a bar.

The teller starts in a baggage room, then wins a post on the trains. He rides as head brake man on a fast food train to New York. The run stops at Detroit to swap cars on its tight clock. Trouble on the road calls for aid past what a lone man can give. The shaggy helper of the tag line holds the key to the fix.
61396-why-i-am-a-vegetarian-an-address-d:
Why I Am a Vegetarian is a talk tract by Howard Moore of Chicago. He spoke it ere the Chicago plant food group in its day. A Dusenberry house of that town brought the small book out in print. His front word of May eighteen ninety five calls it a shot, not a plea. Man sheds old thought forms as ages bloom, that word opens in trope.

Its plea is kin bond of man with all life, that front word holds. Tags from Plutarch, Goldsmith, and Thompson front the talk in rank. One tag calls meat need a coarse wrong thought in plain words there. The talk claims no plan to turn hearers by force of words at all. Half a score of years of crust in minds will not rinse in one talk, he owns.
61600-the-castaways-of-the-flag:
Jules Verne wrote a sequel to the Swiss Family Robinson story, published at New York in 1924. H C Murphy drew its frontispiece. The book is called the final adventures of the Swiss Family Robinson. A preface explains the Robinson tale and its sequel Their Island Home. Chapter one presents the castaways. In England and the mutiny on the Flag follow. A picture caption says resistance was hopeless against a whole crew of mutineers.

Land ahead, a barren shore, and a time of trial test the family. The coming of the Albatross brings change. G Howard Watt published the translation on Broadway. Verne's sequel extends Wyss's tale with his own machinery of adventure.
63701-a-key-into-the-language-of-america:
A help to the tongue of the native folk of New England was first printed in 1643. A fresh form came out at Providence in 1827. It sits in the sets of the Rhode Island Historical Society. Roger Williams stands as the book's known maker in that set. Old spell faults of 1643 were kept as they stood.

Word lists in two rows give the native tongue next to English. Williams learned that tongue in trade and talk with its folk. The book was a key for new men in a new land. Talk of food, kin, trade, and faith fills its lists. A life sketch of Williams goes with this form. Tongue and past fans share its worth.
64893-the-fantasy-fan-volume-1-number-9-:
The Fantasy Fan for May 1934 is one issue of a fan magazine. Charles Hornig, managing editor of Wonder Stories, edited the small sheet. Ten cents bought a copy, a dollar the year, from Elizabeth, New Jersey. Volume one, number nine, stands on the masthead of this issue. Our Readers Say opens the number with letters from the fans.

One reader praises the space given to Lovecraft's horror study here. Supernatural Horror in Literature gets called scholarly and well written there. Another cheers Eando Binder's Ancient Voice for its laughter and relief. Robert Howard's Gods of the North wins praise in a third letter. Clark Ashton Smith outdid himself in the poem Revenant, one fan writes. The March number stands called the best one to date there. Smith's Chinoiserie is named exquisite by another pleased reader.
67502-africa-and-the-american-flag: Africa and the American Flag is a volume in the Appleton catalogue of the eighteen-fifties. The surviving head of the text is the publisher's advertising matter rather than the book itself. Around the title stand pages praising a companion Appleton work on Russia, quoted from the New York Tribune and Courier. Nothing of the volume's own argument or author survives in this opening, beyond its title's promise: Africa considered in relation to the flag of the United States.
68709-the-buccaneer-book-songs-of-the-bl:
The Buccaneer Book: Songs of the Black Flag is a book of sea verse by Alden Noble, printed by the Green Mountain Press in 1908. Its poems sing the pirate life of the old sailing days, in ballad measures meant for chanting rather than quiet reading.

A proem addresses the nameless dead whose keels left no trace save smoke and sorrow. It bids them sleep soundly now that blood is no longer red and life no longer cheap. The contents run through a drinking song, Execution Dock, and the plank. A six-part ballad follows a buccaneer's sailing, meeting, wooing, marriage, sunrise, and parting. Closing pieces treat revenge and being marooned.
70149-under-england-s-flag:
Under England's Flag gathers the memoirs, diary, and correspondence of Charles Boothby, a captain of Royal Engineers, covering the years 1804 to 1809. The last survivors of his family compiled the volume, signing themselves only with initials. A and C Black of London published it.

Boothby was born in 1786 and died in 1846. A frontispiece portrait shows the young officer, and pen and ink sketches illustrate the text. His earlier memoir, A Prisoner of France, had covered his last campaign and captivity. Reviewers praised that book as a manual of soldierly kindness and fine humanity. This companion volume reaches back to his first campaigns under England's flag. Family editing preserved a serving officer's letters and journals from the Napoleonic wars for a later century's readers.
70286-from-flag-to-flag:
From Flag to Flag is a memoir by Eliza McHatton-Ripley, published by D. Appleton and Company in 1889. Its subtitle promises a woman's adventures in the South during the Civil War, in Mexico, and in Cuba. In her note she explains the title: she ran from flag to flag, and here tells why and how.

The years she covers held civil war in the United States, a French conquest of Mexico, and revolt in Cuba. The chapters open at a plantation home in Louisiana, with the fall of New Orleans and the holding of Baton Rouge. Her own small part, long a fireside tale, is set down with pictures of life and facts she judged worth keeping.
7038-personal-experiences-of-s-o-susag:
S O Susag of Minneapolis tells a few of his own experiences to show how pioneer ministers worked and how the Lord worked with them through the Holy Spirit. A photograph from about 1898 shows Susag with his wife and children. His foreword praises the burning passion for souls shown by those early workers in labors, fasting, and prayer, even when their training was limited.

The Holy Spirit gave them an unshaken faith in the Word of God, firm in the most trying and, to man, surprisingly unreasonable cases. Susag prays the book will bring faith and encouragement to souls seeking God when all other help has failed. He regrets waiting so long to write, since incidents fell out of order and many were forgotten.
71728-under-the-mikado-s-flag:
Under the Mikado Flag is a boys war novel by Edward Stratemeyer, published in 1904. It belongs to his Soldiers of Fortune series, listed with On to Pekin in the front. The subtitle calls it a tale of young soldiers of fortune in the east. Its hero Gilbert is detained by Russians and faces troublesome days in Port Arthur.

Chapter heads track the first naval battle, an escape and a fight, and Japanese friends. Snow squalls at sea, orders to lay to, and Korea under its old nickname follow. Gilbert joins the Japanese army and marches toward Ping Yang in the later acts. The Russo Japanese war gives the book its ground and its pace.
77848-defending-his-flag:
Defending His Flag, by Edward Stratemeyer, was first put out as a serial in 1906 and 1907, then printed in book form at Boston in 1907. Its full title adds A Boy in Blue and a Boy in Gray. Stratemeyer wrote the Old Glory books and the Dave Porter books for young readers.

The tale is set in the Civil War, with chapter heads that name signs of war, a trip to Washington, and the advance to Bull Run. One boy serves the Union and one the South, and their paths cross in camp, chase, and fight. Later heads name a stolen horse, a capture, and the landing for Yorktown. Boys of its day got a war story told close to the ground, through young eyes on both sides.
9779-the-black-bag:
Louis Joseph Vance wrote The Black Bag in 1908, a romance of a ruined gentleman's adventures. Chapters follow diversions of a ruined gentleman, a mystery four-wheeler, and below bridge, with Madame L'Intrigante and desperate measures. A primer of progressive crime, stratagems and spoils, and refugees fill the middle acts. Rogues, vagabonds, and adventurers' luck close the chase.

Vance writes with brisk, picaresque verve, favoring disguise, pursuit, and wit. The black bag itself drives the plot from London streets to the Nore. A reader gets a lively Edwardian adventure, full of rogues and rescues, from a master of light suspense.
a-reputed-changeling-or-three-seventh-ye: Charlotte Mary Yonge tells a story of three periods of seven years, two centuries ago, opening with two schoolgirls at Winchester discussing an ugly, ill-favoured boy. The girls call him a changeling, quoting Gay's verse about a fairy who conveyed the true babe away and laid another in its place. Through Goody Madge, Anne Woodford, and Lucy Archfield, the novel tests fairy lore against family feeling, duty, and the slow proof of character.
britannica-1911-baliuag:
Baliuag was a town in the province of Bulacán, on the island of Luzon in the Philippines. It stands on the Quiñgua river, 29 miles by rail north-west of Manila. Its population in 1903 was 21,008, a figure that counts in Bustos, annexed that year after the census was taken.

A branch of the Manila to Dagupan railway served the town. The 1911 Britannica entry calls Baliuag the trade centre of a fertile farming district. Its makers turned out bamboo hats, silk goods, and wares made from native fibres. The entry is short, keeping to the town's place, size, rail link, and trades.
britannica-1911-crag: Crag is a Celtic word for a steep rock, with kin forms in Gaelic, Manx, Welsh, and Scots speech. The 1911 Britannica entry notes it in a host of place names in north England and Scotland. In earth science it fits beds that hold sand full of shells. In the phrase crag and tail it names a hill with a steep rock face on one side and a long slope on the other.
britannica-1911-gadag: Gadag, or Garag, is a town of British India in the Dharwar district of Bombay, 43 miles east of Dharwar town, with 30,652 people in 1901. It is an important junction on the Southern Mahratta railway, trading in raw cotton and in cotton and silk weaving. The town has factories for ginning and pressing cotton and a spinning mill. Its many temples show fine carving, and inscriptions in them carry the place back to the 10th century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-kon:
Ferdinand Konsag was a German Jesuit missionary in the missions of Lower California. Born in Croatia in 1703, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1719. He reached Mexico in 1730 and laboured chiefly in the mission of Lower California. As visitator he oversaw the whole mission with ardent zeal.

Konsag explored the coastal country as far as the Rio Colorado river. His maps, diaries, and letters shaped the later histories of California's missions. Despite delicate health, he achieved far more than seemed possible. He died in 1758, famed as a courageous explorer and cartographer.
doe-osti-17084222-spatial-risk-analysis-:
Thad Haines and Rodrigo Trevizan of Sandia map outage risk across a medium voltage distribution service area in report SAND2026-26823, printed September 2026. The aim is planning where energy storage could best support resilience, meaning keeping power on through disruptions. Work was funded by the Energy Department Office of Electricity, Energy Storage Division.

Feeders in the study area are divided into spatial zones, including zones served by a single feeder, which carry higher risk. Maps score each zone by longest outage, outage counts and durations in 2025 reports, and how much critical infrastructure sits inside it. The layered scores point planners toward the spots where a battery would protect the most value.
doe-osti-17149785-safety-testing-and-des:
William Cureton, Tyler Gerczak, Jesse Werden, and Oak Ridge colleagues report safety testing and destructive examination of two AGR-5/6/7 fuel compacts, in report ORNL/TM-2026/4843 dated September 2026. The compacts hold TRISO particles, tiny coated fuel kernels, from Capsule 5 of the irradiation campaign. Post irradiation examination, shortened to PIE, checks how the fuel held up.

Compact 5-5-3 was heated at 1600 degrees Celsius for about 300 hours as a safety test. It held fission products strongly: no krypton 85 showed above detection limits, and cesium 134 release totaled only 0.045 particle equivalents, with no sign of full particle failure. Silver release stayed small but rose after roughly 100 hours. Compact 5-6-3 was examined as irradiated by leach burn methods, gamma scanning, x ray tomography, and electron microscopy.
doe-osti-17197393-safety-testing-and-des: AGR compacts 5-5-3 and 5-6-3 got their safety tests again, and this DOE report covers the destructive PIE. The pages record the breakage data. The testers get their results. The compacts were tested. The results were breakage. The testing was safety. The data were breakage.
doe-osti-2586985-mil-std-464c-and-mil-st:
Megan Daily of Sandia National Laboratories wrote this evaluation, SAND2025-10567, of the electromagnetic radiation environments in two versions of a military standard. Mil-Std-464, in its C and D revisions, sets electromagnetic environmental effects requirements for systems. Many systems take their radiation environments straight from its tables.

Nuclear weapon systems often start from the standard's ordnance environments, since anything entering Department of Defense custody must be certified safe against hazards of electromagnetic radiation to ordnance under its Table 9. That envelope bundles every source a system might ever meet, including sources irrelevant to a given system. Daily traces which sources actually drive the maximum ordnance levels, band by band. Between the revisions, the environment rose sharply from 2,700 to 3,600 megahertz. The added clarity helps engineers tailor environments to their system and credit shielding honestly.
doe-osti-3001345-optimizing-alabama-s-co:
Kenneth Nemeth of the Southern States Energy Board presents the closeout slides for Project OASIS, award DE-FE0032267, at a meeting on 3 September 2025. Kimberly Sams-Gray and Ben Wernette were co investigators. OASIS tested whether Shelby County, Alabama could store captured carbon dioxide underground, near the National Carbon Capture Center and Plant Gaston. The deck recaps the value chain, and what the project built besides geology data.

Workforce and outreach bulk large. Twenty internships ran at Alabama A&M University. Computer stations were donated for training in seismic software, with Baker Hughes helping. An open house hosted students, and the team engaged the governor and legislators. The technical thread follows site characterisation and the Westover number 2 test well. It was relocated to thin a shale, with mud weight and directional drilling holding the hole stable. Conclusions share the programme's lessons with projects facing folded, faulted terrain.
doe-osti-3001348-optimizing-alabama-s-co:
John Koster, Mitchell Meyer and John Ready of Advanced Resources International deliver the analysis for Project OASIS in August 2025, Task 4.0 of award DE-FE0032267. Kenneth Nemeth of the Southern States Energy Board leads the project, with Ben Wernette as co investigator. The question is whether the Knox Group carbonates under Shelby County, Alabama can hold carbon dioxide for good. Two stratigraphic wells, Westover and the Arco Anschutz bore, supply the evidence, alongside well data.

Formation micro-imager logs revealed bedding and fracture patterns inside the Knox carbonates. Sidewall core sections show veins and fractures threading dolomite, with vuggy pore spaces picked out in blue. Gamma ray, density and sonic logs complete the Westover picture, and a stratigraphic column ties the units both wells met. Valley and Ridge geology makes this harder ground than the coastal plain: the report assembles the rock evidence capacity and risk work stands on.
doe-osti-3001350-optimizing-alabama-s-co:
Kenneth Nemeth, Kimberly Sams-Gray and Ben Wernette of the Southern States Energy Board judge whether Project OASIS is ready for the big league in this Task 6.0 deliverable, dated September 2025, for award DE-FE0032267. CarbonSAFE Phase III demands proof that a site can take 50 million tonnes of carbon dioxide. OASIS studied the Cambro-Ordovician Knox Group, plus the deeper Conasauga and Rome formations, in central Alabama near Plant Gaston, drilling two stratigraphic wells for logs and core.

Scenario analysis compares development paths: storage capacity against available carbon dioxide sources, dynamic modelling of injectivity under three scenarios, well cost estimates and cashflow models with their assumptions tabulated. Samples from the wells were tested in the laboratory, Sample 3203 among them. Static earth models built from the field data frame the verdict on readiness, and what gaps remain. The report is the project's honest self-assessment before asking for Phase III scale funding.
doe-osti-3001352-optimizing-alabama-s-co:
A sober commercialisation plan closes Project OASIS's Task 8.0 in September 2025, written by Kenneth Nemeth's Southern States Energy Board team with Advanced Resources International and Crescent Resource Innovation, under award DE-FE0032267. The geology chapters summarise a deep test well drilled through a repeated, folded section of Cambro-Ordovician carbonates, collecting sidewall core and geophysical data for the storage model. Then the economics take over, and they are unkind.

High capture island construction costs and limited injectivity make the numbers fail; reaching the CarbonSAFE target of 50 million metric tons over 30 years looks challenging on current data. Difficult drilling, constrained capacity and a large area of review needing many wells compound the problem. The plan's advice: smaller single-emitter projects, carbon dioxide use, or piping emissions to better storage elsewhere. Only a cheaper capture plant or a better formation, perhaps the deeper Rome, would revive the big version.
doe-osti-3001481-combining-long-term-obs:
Lynn Russell of Scripps and Ann Fridlind of NASA report for award DE-SC0021983 on Arctic clouds that climate models get wrong. Marine cold air outbreaks, when frigid air pours over warmer ocean, breed stratiform clouds. Their rain and snow processes also steer the extratropical cloud feedback, a leading uncertainty in climate sensitivity. Models show radiative biases in these regimes, worst over the Southern Ocean.

Observations came from the Energy Department's ARM programme, especially the COMBLE campaign in Norway. The team filtered COMBLE data for weather patterns allowing air mass following simulations. The upwind Mount Zeppelin site on Svalbard initialised cases tracked to Andenes. Aerosol data grounded case studies of precipitation across shallow cloud conditions. Those cases then stress tested how models turn cloud water into precipitation. The report, DOE-SCRIPPS-21983-1, ties observations and case studies back to the model errors they are meant to shrink.
doe-osti-3010881-early-career-constraini:
Early career final report for DOE award DE-SC0021191, by Michael Mooney of Colorado State University, covers pinning down the electromagnetic shower energy scale at liquid argon neutrino detectors. Showers from electrons and photons carry DUNE's core oscillation measurements, so their energy scale must be trusted.

The near-far design of DUNE, 1,300 kilometres from Fermilab to South Dakota, cancels many errors, but only if both detectors measure showers the same way. Work-in-progress reconstructions of neutral pion mass anchor the scale in the running Short-Baseline program. The SBND sample held 4.58 and the ICARUS sample 16.2 times ten to the eighteenth protons on target. MicroBooNE data from 2015 to 2021 feeds the same calibration chain.
doe-osti-3013033-disspatch-h2-assessing-:
GTI Energy's final report, dated January 14, 2026, assesses underground hydrogen storage under the DISSPATCH H2 project. The work ran under contract DE-FE0032351 from October 2023 to September 2025. Wing (May) Kwan led as principal investigator. Staff from Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and the University of Oklahoma joined. Storing hydrogen in rock formations could buffer supply for a hydrogen economy. The gas must stay put and stay clean.

The team screened formations such as the Simpson Group and the Red Fork Formation. Red Fork cores proved too tight, with low porosity and permeability. Injection tests thus shifted to Simpson Group samples. Fluid samples from both formations fed microbial studies. Those studies found that hydrogen-eating transformation depends on pressure. Modeling moved the storage concept from technology readiness level 2 to level 4.
doe-osti-3013506-stakeholder-questionnai:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/3748, by Bryan Bozeman, Gbadebo Oladosu, Christopher DeRolph, Debjani Singh, and Paul Matson, dated January 2026, documents a stakeholder questionnaire on fish passage facilities at U.S. hydropower developments. Dams block migrating fish, and passage structures such as ladders and lifts are the standard remedy. Federal inventories of those structures are patchy, so the team went to the industry for the missing facts.

The report explains how the questionnaire defines a unique hydropower feature and a unique fish passage facility, and how its information sections are organized. Distribution ran through the Low Impact Hydropower Institute, the National Hydropower Association, the Electric Utility Cost Group, and DOE's water power office, plus conference networking. A companion user guide helped respondents complete the survey consistently.
doe-osti-3014472-optimizing-alabama-s-co:
Southern States Energy Board's OASIS final report, submitted January 27, 2026, for award DE-FE0032267, covers a CarbonSAFE Phase II study of carbon dioxide storage in Shelby County, Alabama. Kenneth Nemeth, Kimberly Sams Gray, and Benjamin Wernette led the project, running September 2023 to September 2025. The goal was a commercial-scale storage complex for CO2 captured at Plant Gaston and nearby industrial sources, which today have no known viable storage option nearby.

Drilling and core analysis found the carbonate storage matrix tight: peak porosity of 2.5 percent and peak permeability of 1.5 millidarcies in routine sidewall core tests. Storage would therefore rest mainly on fractures, with slow diffusion into porous intervals adding capacity over time. About 2,000 feet of tight carbonate and 1,500 feet of shale above seal the structure.
doe-osti-3018641-machine-learning-for-su:
Elisa Stabilini applied machine learning to superconducting magnet signals in FERMILAB-TM-2888-STUDENT, her report for the 2023 Italian Summer Students program. Emanuela Barzi of Fermilab supervised, with Reed Teyber of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory as co-supervisor. The data came from quench antennas. When a superconducting magnet quenches, antenna signals record the mechanical and electromagnetic events inside. Reading those signals could teach builders how magnets fail. Stabilini's tool was K-means clustering, applied to sort quench events into families.

The clustering code proved robust, separating events reliably in tricky cases. Filtering cleaned the signals before classification. Results pointed to areas worth study. They also suggested directions for improving magnet construction. The work sat inside Berkeley's CCT subscale magnet program, which develops canted-cosine-theta designs. For that program, a way to sort quench traces is leverage. The report documents the method and its limits, as a handoff should.
doe-osti-3363756-identifying-barriers-to:
A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory slide deck by Joachim Seel, Julie Mulvaney Kemp, Anna Cheyette, and colleagues compares how co-located solar and battery projects actually earn money in wholesale power markets. The projects pair solar panels with storage behind one grid connection. The team studies large projects that ran during 2024 across seven regional grid operators and nineteen other balancing areas.

Four samples anchor the analysis: 280 modeled solar-plus-storage projects, a smaller cost-data subset, and two subsets with real operating records from 2020 to 2024. The modeled fleet totals 12.6 gigawatts of solar and 7.3 gigawatts of batteries. Real-world dispatch earns less than optimized dispatch would. In New York's 2024 market, for example, actual operation captured only part of the storage premium that ideal scheduling promised. The deck names market rules and weak price signals as likely barriers.
facing-the-flag:
Verne's Facing the Flag is a novel of a stolen weapon and a pirate stronghold. Jules Verne wrote it as Face au drapeau in 1896. This text is the anonymous American translation first issued in 1897. The engineer Simon Hart narrates much of the tale in his notes.

The contents open at a place called Healthful House. Count d'Artigas arrives, and a kidnapping follows in chapter III. The schooner Ebba carries the captives to Back Cup. Ker Karraje rules that hidden base, and Engineer Serko advises him. Five weeks in Back Cup build toward a naval fight. A battle between the Sword and a tug precedes the climax. Verne mixes invention, sea power, and patriotic peril.
govdocs-archive_org-LinaJriTheFightAgain:
Juri Lina, an Estonian writer, assembled The Fight Against Usury as a history of the condemnation of lending at interest. His authorities run from Plato and Aristotle through the early Church Fathers to Goethe and Wagner. The book is a polemic built from quotations across two thousand years.

Lina marshals the long tradition that treated usury as theft and traces how the ban weakened as modern banking rose. His reading is his own, and the work is controversial, classed by critics with conspiratorial literature. It is held in the archive's collection as it stands: the usury question, polemically told, for readers studying the argument and its sources.
michael-s-crag:
Grant Allen published this novel in Chicago and New York in 1893. It carries more than three hundred and fifty silhouette illustrations by Francis and Alec Carruthers Gould. The opening chapters name a Cornish landlord and the place called Trevennack. Later chapters promise remorse, a strange delusion, and peril by land.

The chapter list shows a plot of danger and rescue on the Cornish coast. Titles like Medical Opinion and A Bold Attempt hint at injury and disputed sanity. Allen keeps the pace of a popular adventure while filling it with coastal scenery. The silhouettes give the book a striking visual character unlike ordinary illustrated novels.
nasa-tm-19660009041-electron-emission-wi:
James F Morris at Lewis Research Center wrote this journal article draft, dated December 28, 1964, on how electrons leave a hot surface. Near a surface, an electron feels a pull called the image potential. Morris studies what changes when that pull is cut off, or terminated, at some point. Transmission coefficients, which give the chance of escape, are part of the study.

Electron emission drives thermionic converters and many vacuum devices. A small change in the surface pull can change the current a great deal. Morris treats the physics in a form suited to a journal of applied physics. The work belongs to the basic research behind power devices that NASA hoped to fly.
personal-experiences-of-s-o-susag:
S. O. Susag wrote his Personal Experiences to show how the pioneer ministers worked, and how, he believed, the Lord worked with them. His foreword praises their burning passion for souls, shown in labours, fasting, and prayer. The book, first published in 1948 at Guthrie, Oklahoma, collects testimonies of outstanding answers to prayer.

A publisher's preface adds that Susag was born at Steinkjer, Norway, in 1862 and came to Minneapolis, where he kept a store before moving to Paynesville, Minnesota, in 1892. Demand kept the little book in print through a fourth edition.
podcast-joerogan-2EgPGQmhWag:
Rogan turns tour guide in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience that roams across world history. The talk moves from ancient empires and the men who conquered them to Martin Luther, the German monk whose protest split the Western church. Few podcast hours cover ground this wide.

Along the way, Rogan links the rise and fall of empires to the lives of bold, ruthless leaders. Luther's stand against Rome becomes a case study in how one person can shake a whole system. The segment works as a fast, opinionated sweep through conquest, faith, and power, told in the show's loose style.
podcast-tuckercarlson-dPEbjKiJ5ag:
Former congressman Matt Gaetz joins Tucker Carlson in Florida for a sharp political talk. They open with a clip from a Jerusalem Post event in Washington. A state official's words set off the discussion.

The title targets Senator Ted Cruz and a hoped-for 2028 run. Gaetz calls that bid delusional. They also discuss the ADL and its role in public debate. Gaetz argues identity politics now infects the right as well. The episode gives his blunt read on party fights that most officials discuss only in private. Neither man softens his words for party leaders.
the-black-bag:
Louis Joseph Vance published an adventure novel in 1908, dedicated to his mother, with illustrations by Thomas Fogarty. Chapter one is called Diversions of a Ruined Gentleman. A later heading says some people have adventures thrust upon them.

Calendar's daughter, an address at 9 Frognall Street, and the mystery of a four-wheeler follow. Chapters move below bridge, to desperate measures, and off the Nore. A primer of progressive crime, stratagems and spoils, and travels with a chaperon promise rogues and vagabonds. Illustration captions show a boy helped to his feet and a man straddling Mulready's body before two others.
the-gold-bag: Carolyn Wells wrote The Gold Bag. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of twenty chapters. The heads open with The Crime in West Sedgwick. They open with The Crawford House. They move through an inquest. They name Florence Lloyd, yellow roses, a will, and Louis's confession. Later heads promise The Owner of the Gold Bag, a midnight train, and Fleming Stone. It is a murder mystery built around a gold bag.
under-the-dragon-flag:
James Allan's Under the Dragon Flag, published at New York in 1898, records his experiences in the Chino-Japanese War. Chapter one begins with apologies for plain writing: he claims no literary skill, only exact and unadorned remembrance of things he witnessed and took part in. A few facts about himself, he says, are necessary first.

Allan was a Lancashire gentleman's son who inherited upwards of eighty thousand pounds from the cotton trade. He ran through the fortune in under four years at Paris gaieties and Monte Carlo gaming tables. Broke and regretful, he stood at ruin's terminus when chance threw him toward China. The memoir's war reporting grows out of that spent fortune.
